summary: Overviews the Portable Document Format, explains its digital signature and encryption mechanisms, and updates the registration of the application/pdf media type. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 8118.

eli5.summary: PDF files look the same on every computer. This note describes them and gives them an official name tag for the internet.

subtitle: Official registration of the PDF file format and its security features.

tldr.problem: The Portable Document Format (PDF) is widely used on the Internet for document exchange but lacked a complete, up-to-date media type registration that documented its digital signature and encryption capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: This document registers the application/pdf media type, overviews the PDF format, and explains the mechanisms for encryption and digital signatures that allow PDF files to be protected and authenticated.

today: RFC 3778 is Informational and has been superseded by RFC 8118. The media type registration remains the standard reference for the application/pdf MIME type on the Internet.

sections.title: PDF and Media Type Registration
sections.content: PDF (Portable Document Format) is a widely used format for document exchange on the Internet since 1993. It preserves document formatting across different computers, operating systems, and networks. PDF documents may contain text, images, graphics, video, audio, hyperlinks, bookmarks, and annotations. The format is used for web documents, email attachments, and electronic document interchange. This RFC updates the registration of the application/pdf media type, which was first registered in 1993. The registration includes information about PDF's design, usage in international standards (PDF/X for prepress, PDF/A for archival), and security features (encryption and digital signatures).
sections.eli5: PDF is a popular way to share documents that always look the same. This explains what PDF is and officially registers its internet name.

sections.title: Design and Evolution
sections.content: PDF was designed to communicate and view printed information electronically across diverse hardware, software, and networks reliably. It uses the same imaging model as PostScript to render text, images, and graphics in a device-independent way. PDF is more structured than PostScript for better interactive performance on screens. The format includes objects beyond page rendering, such as hypertext links and annotations, enabling document collections and collaborative review. PDF has evolved from version 1.0 (1993) through version 1.5 (2003), with each version adding capabilities. The format has been adopted in international standards: ISO 15930-1 (PDF/X) for prepress digital exchange and PDF/A for long-term document preservation.
sections.eli5: PDF was invented to make printed documents work on computers the same way they look on paper. It has grown and now does more, like having clickable links and comments.

sections.title: Encryption and Access Control
sections.content: PDF supports encryption to control access to documents. A document's data decryption keys and permission settings are managed by encryption handlers via an Encryption Dictionary. Different handlers can provide different sets of permissions. Encryption is normally applied to string and stream data, preserving random access to document structure. The data is encrypted using 40 to 128-bit RC4 encryption, with support for other algorithms through decryption filters. Password encryption allows two different passwords: an author password (provides full permissions) and a user password (provides restricted permissions). Public key encryption uses PKCS#7 objects to specify recipients who can open the document. Permissions include the ability to copy text, fill form fields, and print, with enforcement delegated to the viewing application.
sections.eli5: PDF documents can be locked with passwords or encryption so only certain people can read or print them. Different people can have different permissions.

sections.title: Digital Signatures and Authentication
sections.content: PDF digital signatures authenticate the identity of the signer and verify document integrity. A signature is created by computing a digest of document data and storing it in a signature dictionary. To verify, the digest is recomputed and compared with the stored value; differences indicate the document was modified after signing. All bytes of the file are signed except the signature value itself; the range is defined by the ByteRange key. Multiple signers can update and sign the same document using PDF's incremental save feature. When new changes are made, they are appended and the signature digest includes all bytes. Earlier signatures remain valid because they covered the document state when applied. Three signature SubFilter types are defined: adbe.x509.rsa_sha1 (RSA over SHA-1 with PKCS#1), adbe.pkcs7.sha1 (PKCS#7 containing the signature), and adbe.pkcs7.detached (PKCS#7 without encapsulated data). Author signatures can specify what changes are allowed before the signature becomes invalid.
sections.eli5: Someone can sign a PDF to prove they created or approved it. The signature proves that nobody changed the document after signing. Multiple people can sign the same document.

sections.title: Security Concerns and Mitigations
sections.content: PDF files can execute scripts (JavaScript) and load plug-in modules, which pose security risks. Untrusted scripts may access embedded resources or the recipient's system. PDF processors must be careful about executing non-standard plug-ins without prior agreement. JavaScript code can modify PDF appearance, so digital signature validation must account for script execution. Embedded files, scripts, and other material outside the PDF Reference can introduce vulnerabilities. Care must be taken with the source and security of plug-ins. The document provides encryption and digital signature mechanisms to protect PDF integrity and allow recipients to decide whether to trust a file. Processors may track script and plug-in sources and execute only those meeting trustworthiness requirements. Security depends on both the PDF file itself and external resources it references.
sections.eli5: PDF files can be dangerous if they contain malicious scripts or plug-ins. Encryption and digital signatures help protect against tampering and verify who created a PDF.
